title: Do Knowledge-Building Curricula Really Lack Whole Books?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler addresses a surprising line of criticism: some teachers and parents now accuse the knowledge-building curricula she has championed (CKLA, EL Education, Wit & Wisdom, Common Lit 360) of the very flaw she attacked in skills-focused basals, a dearth of whole books. Examining complaints from Houston, Washington D.C., and New York, she argues the charge largely does not hold, since these curricula do include whole texts and books, use connected read-alouds that build knowledge cumulatively, and structure purpose-built texts to spiral vocabulary and concepts. Citing a RAND report, she shows the number of whole books assigned varies widely by school and socioeconomic circumstance, and that complaining parents tend to be highly educated. She concedes middle-schoolers should read more than one novel a year and favours adding books for students who can handle more, while cautioning that quantity is not everything and that some resistance reflects the difficulty of change and teachers' lost autonomy.
points: The surprising complaint is that knowledge-building curricula lack whole books, the same flaw Wexler criticised in excerpt-based basals.
She finds the charge largely unfounded: these curricula include whole texts, and CKLA's connected daily read-alouds build knowledge cumulatively like book chapters.
Purpose-built curriculum texts can be an advantage, spiralling vocabulary and key concepts across contexts and saving schools from buying extra books.
A RAND report shows whole-book assignment varies by school and poverty level, and that many teachers already supplement required curricula with additional books.
Wexler agrees middle-schoolers should read more than one novel a year, favouring adding books over abandoning good curricula, while noting quantity is not everything.
quotes: some teachers and parents—it’s not clear how many—are accusing knowledge-building curricula of exhibiting the same flaws that plague the curricula we’ve criticized
a children’s book you can buy in a store isn’t necessarily better than one written for a particular curriculum.
A short story may be brief, but students are reading an entire work as the author intended it to be read.
the number of whole books assigned by teachers varies from school to school—and that variation depends on lot on socioeconomic circumstances.
even the best curriculum can be implemented in a way that doesn’t work. Poor implementation may be behind some of these complaints.
A teacher’s lack of enthusiasm can easily become contagious.
